scenes.heading: Electron configuration
scenes.sub: Where do the electrons go, and why do the trends happen?
scenes.say: Why are sodium and potassium so reactive? Why does atomic size shrink across a period? It all comes down to which orbitals the electrons occupy, and how strongly the nucleus holds them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Hotel guests book the cheapest room first, not the lowest floor
scenes.science: Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbital first: 4s before 3d
scenes.breaks: hotel prices stay fixed, but orbital energies shift as electrons are added. Once 3d fills, it drops below 4s.
scenes.say: Filling orbitals is like booking hotel rooms by price, not by floor. Guests take the cheapest room first. There's a quirk: one room on floor four, the four s, is cheaper than floor three's d wing. That's the Aufbau principle. And each room holds at most two guests with opposite spins.
scenes.caption: Filling orbitals is like booking hotel rooms by price, not by floor. Guests take the cheapest room first. There's a quirk: the 4s room is cheaper than floor 3's d wing. That's the Aufbau principle. Each room holds at most two guests with opposite spins.

scenes.heading: Three rules for configurations
points: Aufbau: fill lowest energy first (n + l rule)
Pauli: max 2 electrons per orbital, opposite spins
Hund: one per orbital, parallel spins, then pair
scenes.say: Three rules build every configuration. Aufbau: fill the lowest energy first. Pauli: two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins. Hund: like bus seats, take an empty orbital before pairing up. Watch for the two rebels, chromium and copper, which prefer a half-full or full d subshell.

scenes.heading: Transition metal ions: 4s first in, first out
scenes.say: For transition metal ions, four s is first in, first out. Once three d has electrons, it drops below four s in energy. So iron loses its two four s electrons first, giving iron two plus as argon three d six, and iron three plus as argon three d five.
scenes.caption: For transition metal ions, 4s is first in, first out. Once 3d has electrons, it drops below 4s in energy. So Fe loses its two 4s electrons first: Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.

scenes.heading: Effective nuclear charge
parts: net pull felt by the electron
scenes.say: An outer electron doesn't feel the full nuclear charge, because core electrons shield it. Effective nuclear charge is Z minus S, the shielding constant. Core electrons shield well, but electrons in the same shell barely shield at all.
scenes.caption: An outer electron doesn't feel the full nuclear charge, because core electrons shield it. Z_eff = Z − S. Core electrons shield well, but electrons in the same shell barely shield at all.

scenes.heading: Worked example: Slater's rules
scenes.question: Find Z_eff for the valence electron of Na (Z = 11).
scenes.say: For sodium's outer electron, the eight electrons in shell two contribute zero point eight five each, and the two in shell one contribute one each. That gives S equals eight point eight, so Z eff is two point two. Chlorine's is six point one, which is why chlorine is smaller and holds its electrons tighter.
scenes.caption: For Na's outer electron, the 8 electrons in shell 2 contribute 0.85 each, and the 2 in shell 1 contribute 1.00 each. S = 8.80, so Z_eff = 2.20. Cl's is 6.10, which is why Cl is smaller and holds its electrons tighter.

points: Aufbau, Pauli and Hund build configurations
Cr and Cu: half-full or full d
Across a period Z_eff rises: radius falls
Dips: Be beats B, N beats O
scenes.say: Quick recap. Aufbau, Pauli and Hund build configurations. Transition metals lose four s first. Across a period Z eff rises, so radius falls and ionisation energy rises. And remember the dips: beryllium beats boron, nitrogen beats oxygen. Now try the practice questions!
